pluss::note::arange¶

Back to Note Factory API Reference

Signatures¶

Note pluss::note::arange(string_view start, string_view end,
                         std::int64_t step = 1, bool inclusive = true)

A Stepped Run Of Single Characters¶

arange() builds a rank-1 Note whose cells are consecutive single characters, walking the ASCII code-point line from start toward end in increments of step. It is the text analogue of pluss::series::arange — a generator of an ordered sequence — specialised to one-character strings.

Typical uses are building an alphabet or digit axis ("a".."z", "0".."9"), a header row of column letters, or a small fixed lookup of single-character keys, without writing the run out by hand.

Parameters¶

  • start, end — each must be exactly one ASCII character (code point 0x00–0x7F). They are read as byte values; the sequence runs over those values.

  • step — the code-point stride. Must not be 0. A positive step ascends from start; a negative step descends. step may be larger than 1 to skip characters ("a", "c", "e", …).

  • inclusive — whether end itself may appear. It can only ever appear when the stride lands on it exactly; when step steps past end without hitting it, inclusive makes no difference.

The result is always rank 1 and UTF-8 mode. If the direction of step points away from end (ascending step with start already past end, or vice versa), the sequence is empty and a zero-length Note is returned — this is not an error.

Because start and end are ASCII bytes, arange does not walk Unicode letters beyond ASCII; for a non-ASCII character list, build it with make or from_words.

Example 1: A Contiguous Letter Run¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(pluss::note::arange("a", "e")) << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[5], dim=1, numel=5, encoding=utf8)
["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]

Default step = 1, default inclusive = true, so end ("e") is included.

Example 2: A Stride Greater Than One¶

const pluss::Note n = pluss::note::arange("a", "i", 2);
std::cout << n << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[5], dim=1, numel=5, encoding=utf8)
["a", "c", "e", "g", "i"]

Every second character. "i" is reached exactly, so it appears.

Example 3: Excluding The Endpoint¶

pluss::note::print(std::cout, pluss::note::arange("a", "e", 1, false)) << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
["a", "b", "c", "d"]

inclusive = false drops end when the walk would otherwise land on it.

Example 4: inclusive Is Moot When The Stride Overshoots¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(pluss::note::arange("a", "f", 2)) << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[3], dim=1, numel=3, encoding=utf8)
["a", "c", "e"]

The stride goes a, c, e, g — it never lands on "f", so end is absent regardless of inclusive.

Example 5: A Descending Run¶

const pluss::Note n = pluss::note::arange("e", "a", -1);
std::cout << n << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[5], dim=1, numel=5, encoding=utf8)
["e", "d", "c", "b", "a"]

A negative step counts down.

Example 6: A Digit Axis With A Stride¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(pluss::note::arange("0", "9", 3)) << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
["0", "3", "6", "9"]

arange works over any ASCII range, not just letters.

Example 7: A Direction Mismatch Yields An Empty Note¶

const pluss::Note n = pluss::note::arange("e", "a");
std::cout << n << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[0], dim=1, numel=0, encoding=utf8)
[]

A positive step cannot move from "e" toward "a", so the sequence is empty. Not an error — a valid zero-length rank-1 Note.

Example 8: A Zero Step Is Rejected¶

try {
  pluss::note::arange("a", "e", 0);
} catch (const pluss::Error& e) {
  const std::string msg(e.what());
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

pluss::note::arange: step cannot be 0

See Also¶

  • pluss::note::rand: random letters instead of a fixed run.

  • pluss::note::perm: combinations or permutations of a word’s characters.

  • pluss::note::make: write the sequence out explicitly when it is short or non-ASCII.
